name: Spanish Habsburg tercios and the Army of Flanders (1534-1643)

weightNotes.aggression: Offensive in Italy and Germany (Muhlberg 1547, Saint-Quentin 1557, Nordlingen 1634), but in the Low Countries Spain fought a war of position: 'Siege warfare, rather than set-piece battles, dominated the Eighty Years' War' (Army of Flanders page; Parker). Neutral.
weightNotes.maneuver: Deep pike-and-shot squares were slow, and in 1639 just under half of the 77,000-man army sat in 208 small garrisons (Army of Flanders page). Strategic movement along the Spanish Road was impressive but operations were attritional.
weightNotes.flanking: Sleeves of shot protected the squares, and squares could face every direction (Rocroi), but battle plans were frontal; Spanish cavalry was the weak arm: at Rocroi Gassion's horse routed the Spanish left and Enghien rode into the exposed flank (Rocroi page).
weightNotes.siegePreference: The Army of Flanders' war was trace italienne sieges: Ostend held out three years (1601-04) before falling (Ostend page); Parker's Military Revolution thesis is built on this theatre. High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Veteran Spanish tercios in front with mercenary infantry behind (Rocroi); at Nordlingen the commanders fed 'a constant stream of reinforcements' to the Albuch (Nordlingen page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: No distinctive reconnaissance practice is recorded in the sources used; at Rocroi Melo accepted battle before his reinforcements arrived, judging his army the stronger (Rocroi page). Educated guess, middling-low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.gunpowder high quartile 0.356. Sourced refusal to withdraw: at Rocroi 1643 the enveloped tercios held formation against repeated attacks and offered to surrender on terms (Rocroi page). Previous 0.5 came from Guthrie's 3,400 killed of the Spanish battalions, which includes the no-quarter attack after the surrender went wrong, so it is not the loss at the break. Kept under the evidence rule (QA round 4): Rocroi shows formations holding by drill under heavy loss.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Pioneered the integration of pike and arquebus (Cordoba's reforms; tercio of 8 pike and 2 arquebus companies in 1534, the shot ratio rising later; Tercio page). Cavalry and artillery support were weaker, so 0.6.
weightNotes.initiative: Tercios could 'divide into mobile units and even individual melee units without the loss of cohesion' (Tercio page) and detached companies garrisoned and skirmished on their own. But command at army level was fragmented and politicised.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The Spanish Road moved over 123,000 men from Italy to Flanders 1567-1620 through staging posts, and the army ran a military hospital (Spanish Road, Army of Flanders pages; Parker). Lowered because chronic pay arrears caused repeated mutinies and the sack of Antwerp (1576).

summary: Long-service volunteer infantry regiments (tercios) of pikemen and arquebusiers/musketeers, Spanish veterans stiffened by an officer corps of minor nobility, serving with Italian, Walloon and German contingents. They fought in deep pike squares surrounded by sleeves of shot, could split into smaller detachments, and held entrenched positions stubbornly. The Army of Flanders, supplied over the Spanish Road and by sea, spent most of its time besieging or garrisoning fortified towns.
whyItWorked: Training and a high proportion of veterans gave unmatched cohesion; the pike-and-shot combination beat Swiss pike and French gendarmes in the Italian Wars and dominated European infantry for a century. A logistic system spanning Italy, the Alps and the Low Countries kept a large army in the field for 80 years, and at Nordlingen (1634) the tercios on the Albuch broke the Swedish army.
whereItFailed: Money: the crown could not pay, and mutinies (the 1576 sack of Antwerp) cost whole campaigns. Deep squares were slow and vulnerable to the lighter, more firepower-heavy linear tactics and better cavalry of the Dutch, Swedes and French: at Rocroi (1643) the French horse routed the Spanish left, Enghien took the infantry in flank and rear, and massed artillery hammered the squares until they surrendered. The sieges of the Low Countries were slow and the Dutch were never subdued.

sources.title: Parker, The Army of Flanders and the Spanish Road 1567-1659 (Cambridge UP, 2004 ed.)
